title: Reading and searching files
goal: Read big log and config files quickly, find the important lines, and compare two versions of a file.
setup: # Nginx-style access log of the to-do app (40 lines)
# backend log with a few errors

printf '%s\n' '2026-10-20 10:00:01 INFO  backend started on port 8080' '2026-10-20 10:00:05 INFO  connected to database' '2026-10-20 10:05:12 WARN  slow query: 1200 ms' '2026-10-20 10:07:40 ERROR database connection lost' '2026-10-20 10:07:41 INFO  retrying connection' '2026-10-20 10:07:46 ERROR database connection lost' '2026-10-20 10:07:51 INFO  connected to database' '2026-10-20 10:12:03 WARN  slow query: 950 ms' > var/log/backend.log
# frontend log for the live-watch problem
printf '%s\n' '2026-10-20 10:00:02 INFO  frontend started' '2026-10-20 10:03:10 INFO  GET /' '2026-10-20 10:04:55 WARN  api slow (2.1 s)' > var/log/frontend.log
# two versions of an app config
# list of servers with repeats (from 3 inventories)
printf '%s\n' web-02 db-01 web-01 web-02 cache-01 web-01 db-01 web-03 > servers.txt

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Print the last 5 lines of the backend log and count ERROR lines' 'LOG=var/log/backend.log' 'tail -5 $log' 'echo "Errors:"' 'grep ERROR var/log/backend.log | wc -l var/log/backend.log' > report.sh

warmup.q: What is the difference between `/` and `/root`?
warmup.a: `/` is the root directory, the top of all folders. `/root` is the home folder of the root user.

warmup.q: Which command creates `a/b/c` when `a` does not exist yet?
A symlink points to a file. The file is deleted. What happens to the symlink?
warmup.a: It becomes a broken link. `cat` gives `No such file or directory`. A hard link would still work.
It sends error messages (stderr) to `/dev/null`, so they disappear.

problems.title: First look at a big log: head, tail, wc
problems.situation: The to-do app is slow. The team lead asks: "How many requests did Nginx get, and what were the first and the last ones?" The access log is too big to read with `cat`.
task: Count the lines of `var/log/nginx/access.log` with `wc -l`.
Show the first 3 lines with `head`.
Show the last 2 lines with `tail`.
Show only lines 10 to 12 (use `head` and `tail` together with a pipe).
Show the same file with line numbers using `nl`, but only the first 3 lines.
hints: `head -n N` shows the first N lines. `tail -n N` shows the last N lines.
For lines 10-12: take the first 12 lines, then the last 3 of those.

explanation.meaning: Counts lines. Prints the number and the file name.
First 3 lines. Without `-n`, head shows 10 lines.
Last 2 lines. Without `-n`, tail shows 10 lines.
The pipe `|` sends the first 12 lines into `tail`, which keeps the last 3.
Number lines. Like `cat -n`, but skips empty lines by default.

mistakes: Running `cat` on a huge log. The terminal fills with text and the user cannot read it. Use `head`, `tail` or `less`.
Writing `head -3n file`. The correct form is `head -n 3 file` (or the short `head -3 file`).
Expecting `wc -l < file` to print the file name. With `<` it prints only the number (useful in scripts).
problems.interview_say: For a big log I never use `cat`. I use `wc -l` to see the size, `head` and `tail` to see the start and the end, and `less` to scroll and search.
problems.try_yourself: Run `wc -l < var/log/nginx/access.log` and `wc -c var/log/nginx/access.log`. What is different?

problems.title: Watch a log live with tail -f
problems.situation: The frontend pod restarts again and again. The user wants to see new log lines the moment they are written, while a teammate tests the app.
task: Open a **second** terminal window. In it, run `tail -f ~/bash-practice/day02/var/log/frontend.log`.
In the first terminal, add a line: `echo "2026-10-20 10:15:00 ERROR cannot reach api" >> var/log/frontend.log`.
Watch the new line appear in the second terminal. Stop `tail -f` with `Ctrl+C`.
Now show only the last 3 lines once: `tail -n 3 var/log/frontend.log`.
Open the log in `less`. Press `G` (end), `g` (start), `/ERROR` (search), `n` (next match), `q` (quit).
hints: `-f` means follow: tail keeps the file open and prints new lines.
`>>` adds to the end of a file. `>` would delete the old content first.
Stop a running command with `Ctrl+C`. In `less`, `q` quits.
solution: # Here we start it in the background for 2 seconds to show the effect:
echo "2026-10-20 10:15:00 ERROR cannot reach api" >> var/log/frontend.log
kill "$TAIL_PID"                      # same as pressing Ctrl+C in terminal 2

explanation.meaning: Follow the file. New lines are printed as soon as they are written.
Start with 0 old lines, only show new ones.
Run in the background, so the script can continue. The user does not need this in a second terminal.
Process ID of the last background command.
Append: add the line at the end of the file.
Scroll a file page by page. `G` end, `g` start, `/word` search, `n` next, `q` quit.

problems.expected_output:
2026-10-20 10:15:00 ERROR cannot reach api
--- last 3 lines ---
2026-10-20 10:03:10 INFO  GET /
2026-10-20 10:04:55 WARN  api slow (2.1 s)
2026-10-20 10:15:00 ERROR cannot reach api
mistakes: Using `>` instead of `>>`. The whole log is replaced by one line.
Closing the terminal window to stop `tail -f`. Use `Ctrl+C`.
Using `tail -f` on a log that is rotated (renamed). Use `tail -F` (capital F) to follow the new file after rotation.
problems.interview_say: I use `tail -f` to watch a log live while I reproduce the problem. For logs that rotate I use `tail -F`. In Kubernetes the same idea is `kubectl logs -f`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `tail -f var/log/frontend.log | grep ERROR` in terminal 2, then add an INFO line and an ERROR line from terminal 1. Which ones appear?

problems.title: Find the errors with grep
problems.situation: The backend lost its database connection this morning. The user must show the team only the error lines, count them, and see what happened just before the first error.
task: Show all lines with `ERROR` in `var/log/backend.log`.
Count them with `grep -c`.
Show the line numbers of the WARN lines with `grep -n`.
Show lines that do **not** contain `INFO` with `grep -v`.
Search for `error` without caring about upper or lower case (`-i`), and count.
hints: `-c` counts, `-n` adds line numbers, `-v` inverts (non-matching lines), `-i` ignores case.

explanation.meaning: Print lines that contain the text `ERROR` (case-sensitive).
Print only the number of matching lines.
Show the line number before each match.
Invert: show lines that do NOT match.
Ignore case: `error`, `Error` and `ERROR` all match.

problems.expected_output:
2026-10-20 10:07:40 ERROR database connection lost
2026-10-20 10:07:46 ERROR database connection lost
2
3:2026-10-20 10:05:12 WARN  slow query: 1200 ms
8:2026-10-20 10:12:03 WARN  slow query: 950 ms
2026-10-20 10:05:12 WARN  slow query: 1200 ms
2026-10-20 10:07:40 ERROR database connection lost
2026-10-20 10:07:46 ERROR database connection lost
2026-10-20 10:12:03 WARN  slow query: 950 ms
2
mistakes: Wrong case: `grep error var/log/backend.log` prints nothing, because the log uses `ERROR`. Add `-i`.
Putting the file first: `grep var/log/backend.log ERROR` gives `grep: ERROR: No such file or directory`. The pattern comes first.
Thinking `grep -c` counts words. It counts lines. Two errors on one line count as 1.

checks.expect: grep: ERROR: No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: I use `grep` to filter logs: `-i` to ignore case, `-v` to remove noise, `-n` for line numbers and `-c` to count. Day 10 adds context options like `-B` and `-A`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `grep -B 1 ERROR var/log/backend.log`. What does `-B 1` add? Try `-A 1` too.

problems.title: Unique server names: sort and uniq
problems.situation: Three teams sent lists of servers that need a security patch. The lists were joined into `servers.txt`, so some names repeat. The user needs a clean list and wants to know which servers were reported more than once.
task: Show `servers.txt` with `cat`.
Print the names sorted A-Z.
Print each name only once (sorted).
Print how many times each name appears (use `uniq -c`).
Show only the names that appear more than once (use `uniq -d`).
hints: `uniq` only removes repeats that are next to each other. So sort first.
`sort servers.txt | uniq -c` counts; `sort servers.txt | uniq -d` shows duplicates only.

explanation.meaning: Sort lines alphabetically (A-Z).
Sort and keep each line once.
Count each group of equal lines. The count comes first.
Print only lines that repeat.

problems.expected_output:
web-02
db-01
web-01
web-02
cache-01
web-01
db-01
web-03
--- sorted ---
cache-01
db-01
db-01
web-01
web-01
web-02
web-02
web-03
--- unique ---
cache-01
db-01
web-01
web-02
web-03
--- count ---
      1 cache-01
      2 db-01
      2 web-01
      2 web-02
      1 web-03
--- reported more than once ---
db-01
web-01
web-02
mistakes: Running `uniq servers.txt` without sorting. `web-02` stays twice because the two copies are not next to each other.
Expecting `uniq -c` output to be sorted by count. Add `| sort -rn` for that (Day 12).
problems.interview_say: `uniq` only removes neighbour duplicates, so I always `sort` first. `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` is my standard way to count things, like IPs in a log.
problems.try_yourself: Run `sort servers.txt | uniq -u`. What does `-u` on uniq show?

problems.title: What changed in the config? diff
problems.situation: After a deploy, the backend cannot reach the database. Someone changed the config. The user has the old file `app-v1.conf` and the new file `app-v2.conf` and must find the exact changes.
task: Compare the two files with `diff app-v1.conf app-v2.conf`.
Compare again with `diff -u` (the format used by git).
Check the exit code with `echo $?` right after `diff`.
hints: In plain `diff`, `<` lines come from the first file and `>` lines from the second file.
In `diff -u`, `-` means removed and `+` means added.
`diff` exits with 0 when the files are the same and 1 when they are different.
solution: diff -u app-v1.conf app-v2.conf | tail -n +3    # skip the 2 header lines with dates

explanation.meaning: Show lines that are different. `2,3c2,3` means lines 2-3 were changed (c = change).
`<` = line from the first file, `>` = line from the second file.
Exit code of diff: 0 = same, 1 = different, 2 = error (for example a missing file).
Unified format, like `git diff`: `-` removed, `+` added, with some lines around for context.
Print from line 3 to the end. Here it hides the header with file dates.

problems.expected_output:
2,3c2,3
< db_host=db.internal
< db_pool=10
---
> db_host=db-new.internal
> db_pool=20
exit code: 1
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 port=8080
-db_host=db.internal
-db_pool=10
+db_host=db-new.internal
+db_pool=20
 log_level=info
 cache=on
mistakes: Thinking exit code 1 from `diff` means the command failed. For `diff`, 1 only means "files are different". In a script with `set -e`, this stops the script.
Mixing up the order. `diff old new` shows `>` for the new lines. Always put the old file first.
problems.interview_say: I compare configs with `diff -u old new`. The changed lines show the bug quickly; here `db_host` and `db_pool` changed.
problems.try_yourself: Run `diff app-v1.conf app-v1.conf; echo $?`. Then try `diff app-v1.conf nofile.conf; echo $?`.

problems.title: Find the bug: the log report script
problems.situation: A teammate wrote `report.sh` to print the last 5 lines of the backend log and the number of errors. It hangs, and the error count looks wrong.
task: Look at the script with `cat report.sh`. Do **not** run it yet (it waits for input forever).
Find 2 bugs: one variable name problem and one wrong pipe.
Fix the script and run it with `bash report.sh`.
hints: Bash variable names are case-sensitive. `LOG` and `log` are two different variables.
When `$log` is empty, the command is just `tail -5`, which reads from the keyboard and waits.
In a pipe, `wc -l` must read from the pipe, so do not give it a file name: `grep ERROR file | wc -l`, or use `grep -c`.
solution: # Print the last 5 lines of the backend log and count ERROR lines

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: the script set `LOG` but used `$log`. The empty variable made `tail` wait for keyboard input. Quotes also protect paths with spaces.
Bug 2: `wc -l file` ignored the pipe and counted all lines of the file. `grep -c` counts only matching lines.

problems.expected_output:
2026-10-20 10:07:40 ERROR database connection lost
2026-10-20 10:07:41 INFO  retrying connection
2026-10-20 10:07:46 ERROR database connection lost
2026-10-20 10:07:51 INFO  connected to database
2026-10-20 10:12:03 WARN  slow query: 950 ms
Errors:
2
mistakes: Running the broken script: it hangs with no message. Press `Ctrl+C` to stop it.
Counting with `wc -l var/log/backend.log` after the pipe: the output is `8 var/log/backend.log`, the total lines, not the errors.
problems.interview_say: Variable names in bash are case-sensitive, and an empty variable can change a command completely. I use ShellCheck and `set -u` to catch this.
problems.try_yourself: Add `set -u` as the second line of the broken script and run it. What error do you get now?

interview.q: What is the difference between `head`, `tail` and `tail -f`?
interview.a: `head` shows the first lines, `tail` the last lines, and `tail -f` keeps the file open and prints new lines as they are written.

interview.q: How do you count the error lines in a log file?
interview.a: `grep -c ERROR app.log`. Or `grep ERROR app.log | wc -l`.
`uniq` only removes duplicate lines that are next to each other. `sort` puts equal lines together first.

interview.q: How do you see what changed between two config files?
interview.a: `diff -u old.conf new.conf`. Lines with `-` were removed and lines with `+` were added.

interview.q: Why not use `cat` for a 2 GB log file?
interview.a: It prints everything to the screen and is slow. `less` lets the user scroll and search, and `tail` or `grep` show only the useful part.

recap.meaning: Scroll and search a file (q quits)
From line N to the end
Count / line numbers / invert / ignore case
